author: ch402

author: ch402

Jotting down a critique in 5 minutes is just very different. The negative externalities of these fast critiques tend to be higher, and the positive value lower.

Twitter incentivizing these quick critiques, combined with a lower trust environment, is a messy combination.

text: Every model is its own entire world of beautiful structure waiting to be discovered, if only we care to look.

author: ch402
text: I wish people would spend more time looking at the models we create though. It's like we're launching expeditions with complex equipment to reach more and more remote islands and tall mountains... and the biology stops at measuring the size and weight of the animals we find.

author: ch402
text:
This aesthetic most obviously applies to interpretability (and explicitly animates https://t.co/1C8ipWMsqA and https://t.co/xVq6Nez7YG). But I think it applies to deep learning more broadly.

Training larger models is an expedition to a remote island to see the organisms there.

author: ch402
text: People often complain that modern ML is throwing GPUs at problems without new research ideas. This is like finding evolution ugly because it's just a simple algorithm run for a very long time.

author: ch402
text: My tools are those of a mathematician, but my aesthetic is that of an early natural scientist.

author: ch402
text: For example, I was very excited about using group theory to encode symmetry in neural networks. But it turns out gradient descent can *discover* group convolutions (https://t.co/ZmVhjE7216). I think that's actually way more beautiful!

author: ch402
text: I used to really want ML to be about complex math and clever proofs. But I've gradually come to think this is really the wrong aesthetic to bring.

author: ch402
text:
The elegance of ML is the elegance of biology, not the elegance of math or physics.

Simple gradient descent creates mind-boggling structure and behavior, just as evolution creates the awe inspiring complexity of nature.

Another frame:

Close relationships are a powerful way to reinforce/solidify/ossify ones identity.

I'm sure I'll realize my present beliefs are wrong in a hundred ways. But I think I have roughly the right values.

So I want relationships to solidify my values, not my beliefs.

author: ch402
text:
What if you step behind a veil of ignorance about your views and ask what kind of traits you want in someone you want to make proud?

Someone being proud of you for values and process feels more robust, veil of ignorance-consistent, and probably ultimately more meaningful.

author: ch402
text:
So, what should one look for in friendships and other relationships, such that integrity won't be compromised?

One answer is "people that you genuinely endorse wanting to make proud." But I think it's easy for that to become "people who agree with your present views."

author: ch402
text: But it's easy for this to lead to situations where one of the strongest psychological forces I know is directly in conflict with my integrity. I've definitely experienced cases where I've struggled with this.

The truth is, part of me _really_ cares what my close friends think of me. (And when I'm dating someone, it's hard to articulate just how much I want to make them proud of me.)
